# Project Summary

# Set-Up Chunks

## Loading packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(lme4)
```

## Loading data sets

```{r}
# Saving Excel data to variables with read_excel
Height_Data_Raw = read_excel(
  "Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
  sheet = "Seedling Heights"
  )

Moist_Data_Raw = read_excel(
  "Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
  sheet = "Soil Moisture"
  )

SPAD_Data_Raw = read_excel(
  "Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
   sheet = "SPAD", na = "NA")
```

# 1. Cleaning Data with dplyr

## 1.1. Cleaning SPAD Data

```{r}
# Visual check to see if data looks as expected
SPAD_Data_Raw

# Cleaning SPAD data
SPAD_Data = SPAD_Data_Raw |>
  
  # Filtering out NA rows (there's a billion for some reason) with filter()
  filter(is.na(Treatment) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Creating new column for sapling number with separate()
  separate(Tag_Num,
           c("Tag_Num", "Sapling_Num"), 
           3, extra = "merge", fill = "right"
  ) |>
  
  # Converting Sapling_Num into characters and adding NA values where applicable
  # with mutate() and case_when()
  mutate(Sapling_Num = case_when(
    Sapling_Num == "A1" ~ "A",
    Sapling_Num == "A2" ~ "B",
    Sapling_Num == "A3" ~ "C",
    is.na(Sapling_Num) == TRUE ~ NA
    )
  )

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data

# Removing QAQC columns to the right of Notes by identifying its column number with which() and then selecting only the columns to the left
Notes_colnum_SPAD = which(colnames(SPAD_Data) == "Notes")
SPAD_Data = SPAD_Data[1:16]

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data

# Creating column of unique identifier numbers with mutate()
SPAD_Data = SPAD_Data |>
  mutate(ID_num = row_number())

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data

# Converting Leaf columns into Leaf_Num column with pivot_longer()
SPAD_Data = SPAD_Data |>
  pivot_longer(names_to = "Leaf_Num", values_to = "SPAD_Value", cols = 9:14) |>
  
  # Removing "Leaf" from Leaf_Num with separate()
  separate(Leaf_Num,
    c("Leaf", "Leaf_Num"), 
    4, extra = "merge", fill = "right"
  ) |>
  
  # Removing Leaf with select()
  select(-Leaf)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data

# Blanket fix for each data type that's wrong with mutate()
SPAD_Data = SPAD_Data |>
  mutate(Tag_Num = as.integer(Tag_Num)) |>
  mutate(Num_leaves = as.integer(Num_leaves)) |>
  mutate(Leaf_Num = as.integer(Leaf_Num))
```

## 1.2. Cleaning Soil Moisture Data

```{r}
# Visual check to see if data looks as expected
Moist_Data_Raw

# Cleaning soil moisture data
Moist_Data <- Moist_Data_Raw |> 
  
  # Removing excess NA rows with filter()
  filter(is.na(Treatment) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Changing "NA" to actual native NA value with mutate() and case_when()
  mutate(VWC1_perc = case_when(
    VWC1_perc == "NA" ~ NA,
    VWC1_perc != "NA" ~ VWC1_perc
  )
  ) |>
  mutate(PER1_ms = case_when(
    PER1_ms == "NA" ~ NA,
    PER1_ms != "NA" ~ PER1_ms
  )
  ) |>
  mutate(VWC2_perc = case_when(
    VWC2_perc == "NA" ~ NA,
    VWC2_perc != "NA" ~ VWC2_perc
  )
  ) |>
  mutate(PER2_ms = case_when(
    PER2_ms == "NA" ~ NA,
    PER2_ms != "NA" ~ PER2_ms
  )
  ) |>
  mutate(VWC3_perc = case_when(
    VWC3_perc == "NA" ~ NA,
    VWC3_perc != "NA" ~ VWC3_perc
  )
  ) |>
  mutate(PER3_ms = case_when(
    PER3_ms == "NA" ~ NA,
    PER3_ms != "NA" ~ PER3_ms
  )
  )

# Visual verification
Moist_Data

# Removing QAQC columns to the right of Notes by identifying its column number with which() and then selecting only the columns to the left
Notes_colnum_Moist = which(colnames(Moist_Data) == "Notes")
Moist_Data = Moist_Data[1:12]

# Visual verification
Moist_Data

# Creating column of unique identifier numbers with mutate()
Moist_Data = Moist_Data |>
  mutate(ID_num = row_number())

# Visual verification
Moist_Data

# Converting VWC/PER columns into VWC_or_PER and value columns with pivot_longer()
Moist_Data = Moist_Data |>
  pivot_longer(names_to = "VWC_or_PER", values_to = "value", cols = 6:11) |>
  
  # Removing tail end of name from VWC_or_PER with separate()
  separate(VWC_or_PER,
           c("VWC_or_PER", "type"), 
           "_"
  ) |>
  
  # Separating VWC_or_PER again with separate() to create a new measure_num column
  separate(VWC_or_PER,
           c("VWC_or_PER", "measure_num"),
           3, extra = "merge", fill = "right"
  ) |>
  
  # Removing type and ID_num columns with select()
  select(-type, -ID_num)

# Visual verification
Moist_Data

# Blanket fixing data types with mutate()
Moist_Data = Moist_Data |>
  mutate(measure_num = as.integer(measure_num)) |>
  mutate(value = as.double(value))

# Visual verification
Moist_Data
```

## 1.3. Cleaning Height Data

```{r}
# Visual check to see if data looks as expected
Height_Data_Raw
  
# Cleaning Height_Data
Height_Data = Height_Data_Raw |>
  
  # Remove NA rows
  filter(is.na(Treatment) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Changing alphanumeric Sapling_AB_etc values to characters
  mutate(Sapling_AB_etc = case_when(
    Sapling_AB_etc == "A1" ~ "A",
    Sapling_AB_etc == "A2" ~ "B",
    Sapling_AB_etc == "A3" ~ "C",
    is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == TRUE ~ NA
    )
  ) |>
  
  # Removing that one random NA value in Dead_Alive
  filter(is.na(Dead_Alive) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Removing any treatment IDs that are incorrect
  filter(Treatment %in% c("AC", "DT", "NR", "OS"))

# Visual verification
Height_Data

# Removing QAQC data
Notes_colnum_Height = which(colnames(Height_Data) == "Notes")
Height_Data = Height_Data[1:10]

# Visual verification
Height_Data

# Blanket fixing data types with mutate()
Height_Data = Height_Data |>
  mutate(Tag_Num = as.integer(Tag_Num))

# Visual verification
Height_Data
```

# 2. Statistical Analysis

## 2.1. Removing data from sampling day 2

The rainstorm that occurred between sampling dates may be introducing some noise to our data. For the sake of simplicity I'm going to focus on day 1 only (for now).

```{r}
# Removing day 2 data from Moist_Data_Clean with filter()
Moist_Data_Clean = Moist_Data |>
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date)) |>
  filter(Date == "2026-10-08")

# Visual verification
Moist_Data_Clean

# Removing day 2 data from SPAD_Data_Clean with filter()
SPAD_Data_Clean = SPAD_Data |>
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date)) |>
  filter(Date == "2026-10-08")

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_Clean

# Removing day 2 data from Moist_Data_Clean with filter()
Height_Data_Clean = Height_Data |>
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date)) |>
  filter(Date == "2026-10-08")

# Visual verification
Height_Data_Clean
```

## 2.2. Regression Testing with SPAD_Value \~ VWC

### 2.2.1. Combining SPAD and Soil Moisture Data

```{r}
# Cleaning up soil moisture data more to prep it for combination
Moist_condensed = Moist_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Removing PER measurements with filter()
  filter(VWC_or_PER == "VWC") |>
  
  # Condensing VWC measurements to an average of the three measurements with
  # summarise()
  group_by(Treatment, Block) |>
  mutate(
    VWC = mean(as.double(value), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  
  # Removing excess columns with select()
  select(-VWC_or_PER, -measure_num, -value) |>
  
  # Removing duplicate rows with distinct()
  distinct(VWC, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  
  # Removing Block 4 Natural Recruits due to them having no data
  filter(is.na(VWC) == FALSE)

# Visual verification
Moist_condensed

# Cleaning up SPAD data more to prep it for combination, defaulting to Alive
# data set since dead plants have no SPAD value
SPAD_condensed = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  
  # Removing dead plants with filter()
  filter(Num_leaves > 0) |>
  
  # Removing Leaf_Num with select() so it doesn't complicate our math
  select(-Leaf_Num) |>
  
  # Creating mean SPAD measurement for each plant with mutate()
  group_by(Treatment, Block) |>
  mutate(SPAD_Value = mean(SPAD_Value, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  
  # Removing duplicate rows with distinct()
  distinct(SPAD_Value, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Visual verification
SPAD_condensed

# Combining tibbles with left_join() to blend identical columns
Moist_SPAD_combined = left_join(Moist_condensed, SPAD_condensed,
  join_by(Block, Treatment)
  ) |>
  
  # Removing NA values
  filter(is.na(SPAD_Value) == FALSE)

# Visual verification
Moist_SPAD_combined
```

### 2.2.2. Initial Visualization of SPAD_Value \~ VWC

```{r}
# Generating scatter plot with a best-fit line using ggplot() + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
Moist_SPAD_combined |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = SPAD_Value) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Mean volumetric water content (as a percentage)",
    y = "Mean SPAD value",
  )
```

Scatter plot of mean SPAD value compared to mean volumetric water content across all treatment types. A line-of-best-fit is fitted to the data and highlighted in blue. Initial visualizations do show impact from outliers in the data, but there may be a weak positive relationship between the two measurements. We will investigate the outliers and remove them if necessary.

```{r}
# Visualizing data to investigate outliers
Moist_SPAD_combined

# Since the two don't have tag numbers we'll remove them with filter()
Moist_SPAD_Alive = Moist_SPAD_combined |>
  filter(is.na(Tag_Num) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Removing extraneous columns with select()
  select(VWC, Block, Treatment, SPAD_Value)

# Visual verification
Moist_SPAD_Alive

# Redoing scatter plot with ggplot() + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
Moist_SPAD_Alive |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = SPAD_Value) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Mean volumetric water content (as a percentage)",
    y = "Mean SPAD value",
  )
```

Scatter plot of mean SPAD value compared to mean volumetric water content across all treatment types. A line-of-best-fit is fitted to the data and highlighted in blue. There may be a weak positive relationship between the two measurements suggested by the trend of the data about the line-of-best-fit. We can explore this now with a regression.

### 2.2.3. Checking Prerequisites for a Linear Regression

```{r}
# Creating mixed effect model with plot as a random effect and treatment as a fixed effect using lmer()
SPAD_Moist_IntME_Model = lmer(
  SPAD_Value ~ VWC * Treatment + (1|Block),
  data = Moist_SPAD_Alive)

# Viewing summary of model with summary()
summary(SPAD_Moist_IntME_Model)

# Creating mixed effect model again with lmer() but removing interaction with Treatment
SPAD_Moist_NoIntME_Model = lmer(
  SPAD_Value ~ VWC + Treatment + (1|Block),
  data = Moist_SPAD_Alive)

# Viewing summary of model with summary()
summary(SPAD_Moist_NoIntME_Model)
```

Since there was no significance found in the initial lmer() model accounting for interactions with treatment, we will move on with the second model.

```{r}
# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot for our model with plot()
plot(SPAD_Moist_NoIntME_Model)

# Checking normality of SPAD_Value with hist()
hist(x = Moist_SPAD_combined$SPAD_Value)
```

Our data have sufficient homogeneity of distribution but appear to be heavily skewed on our histogram. Since our sample size is so small, we will still continue with a simple regression test.

### 2.2.4. Conducting Regression Test

```{r}
# Reviewing summary of linear model with summary()
summary(SPAD_Moist_NoIntME_Model)
```

A model of SPAD value as a function of VWC with block integrated as a random effect and no interactions with treatment showed no significant relationship between the two measurements (p \> 0.05). We thus cannot reject our null hypothesis and lack support for a weakly positive relationship. At the very least, VWC alone is not the primary driver of plant health seemingly. We will conduct an identical regression for plant height to explore this further.

### 2.2.5. Visualizing Regression Results

```{r}
# Generating scatter plot with no best-fit line using ggplot() + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
Moist_SPAD_Alive |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = SPAD_Value) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(label = c("p > 0.05"),
    x = 0.75, y = 36) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Mean volumetric water content (as a percentage)",
    y = "Mean SPAD value",
  )
```

Scatter plot of mean SPAD value compared to mean volumetric water content across all treatment types. Results of a simple regression are displayed on the plot (p = \>0.05). There is no clear indication of a weakly positive relationship between VWC and SPAD value. This could be the result of VWC interacting with other environmental factors but could equally be a function of soil water content being insufficient to support oak sapling development or other stochastic effects.

## 2.3. Regression Testing with Plant Height \~ VWC

### 2.3.1. Combining Height and VWC data

```{r}
# Cleaning Height data for combination, again selecting for live plants only with filter()
Height_condensed = Height_Data_Clean |>
  filter(Seedling_Ht_cm > 0) |>
  
  # Taking mean of plant heights across each treatment
  group_by(Block, Treatment) |>
  mutate(Seedling_Ht_cm = mean(Seedling_Ht_cm)) |>
  
  # Removing duplicated values with distinct()
  distinct(Seedling_Ht_cm, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Visual verification
Height_condensed

# Combining tibbles with left_merge()
Height_Moist_combined = left_join(Moist_condensed, Height_condensed,
  join_by(Block, Treatment)
  )

# Visual verification
Height_Moist_combined

# Removing NA row with filter()
Height_Moist_combined = Height_Moist_combined |>
  filter(is.na(Seedling_Ht_cm) == FALSE)

# Visual verification
Height_Moist_combined
```

### 2.3.2. Initial Visualization of Height \~ VWC

```{r}
# Generating scatter plot with a best fit line using ggplot() + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
Height_Moist_combined |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = VWC, y = Seedling_Ht_cm) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x = "Volumetric Water Content (as a percentage)",
    y = "Plant Height (in cm)"
  )
```

Scatter plot of mean seedling height (in cm) compared to mean volumetric water content across all treatment types. A line-of-best-fit is fitted to the data and highlighted in blue. There does not appear to be any clear relationship between seedling height and VWC, seeing as our data do not correlate with the line-of-best-fit closely at all. We will confirm this with a simple regression test.

### 2.3.3. Checking Prerequisites for A Linear Regression

```{r}
# Creating mixed effect model with plot as a random effect and treatment as a fixed effect using lmer()
Height_Moist_IntME_Model = lmer(
  Seedling_Ht_cm ~ VWC * Treatment + (1|Block),
  data = Height_Moist_combined)

# Viewing summary of model with summary()
summary(Height_Moist_IntME_Model)

# Creating mixed effect model again with lmer() but removing interaction with Treatment
Height_Moist_NoIntME_Model = lmer(
  Seedling_Ht_cm ~ VWC + Treatment + (1|Block),
  data = Height_Moist_combined)

# Viewing summary of model with summary()
summary(Height_Moist_NoIntME_Model)
```

Since there was no significance found in the initial lmer() model accounting for interactions with treatment, we will move on with the second model.

```{r}
# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot for our model with plot()
plot(Height_Moist_NoIntME_Model)

# Checking normality of SPAD_Value with hist()
hist(x = Height_Moist_combined$Seedling_Ht_cm)
```

Our data can be assumed to be normal due to the small sample size and relative shape of the graph, but there is not homogeneity of variance. We will redraw the model with log transformations and redo these checks.

```{r}
# Redoing model with log() transformations
Height_Moist_NoIntME_Model = lmer(
  log(Seedling_Ht_cm) ~ log(VWC) + Treatment + (1|Block),
  data = Height_Moist_combined)

# Checking residuals vs. fitted plot for our model with plot()
plot(Height_Moist_NoIntME_Model)

# Checking normality of SPAD_Value with hist()
hist(x = Height_Moist_combined$Seedling_Ht_cm)
```

With our homogeneity of variance improved, we can now conduct a simple regression test.

### 2.3.4. Conducting Simple Regression Test

```{r}
# Reading summary table of our model with summary()
summary(Height_Moist_NoIntME_Model)
```

A model of seedling height as a function of VWC with block integrated as a random effect and no interactions with treatment showed no significant relationship between the two measurements (p \> 0.05). We thus cannot reject our null hypothesis and lack support for a weakly positive relationship. This reaffirms what we identified in 2.2 in terms of VWC not being the primary driver of plant health. Whether this is due to stochastic effects or an indicator of a deeper relationship with another variable needs further exploration

## 2.4. ANOVA Testing on Leaf Count

### 2.4.1. Cleaning SPAD Data to Remove Extra Saplings in Each Plot

```{r}
# Filtering out data with multiple saplings with filter()
SPAD_Data_multiple = SPAD_Data_Clean |>
  group_by(Tag_Num) |>
  filter(is.na(Sapling_Num) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Selecting only the sapling with the most leaves from each tag with slice_max()
  slice_max(Num_leaves) |>
  
  # Removing duplicate stragglers with distinct()
  distinct(Tag_Num, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_multiple

# Generating intermediate tibble without multiple saplings using filter()
SPAD_Data_temp = SPAD_Data_Alive |>
  filter(is.na(Sapling_Num) == TRUE)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_temp

# Reconstructing main tibble by reattaching SPAD_Data_multiple to SPAD_Data_temp with bind_rows()
SPAD_Data_no_multiple = bind_rows(SPAD_Data_temp, SPAD_Data_multiple)

# Visual verification
SPAD_Data_no_multiple
```

I defaulted to SPAD_Data_Alive because dead leaves don't have SPAD values.

### 2.3.2. Checking Prerequisites for an ANOVA

```{r}
# Generating box plot with ggplot() + geom_boxplot() for Alive data
SPAD_Data_no_multiple |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = Num_leaves) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Treatment), color = "black") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(x = "Treatment",
       y = "Number of leaves",
       title = "Number of leaves across all living plants per treatment"
  )
```

Open sky has a colossal outlier that has to go before we can continue. It is also worth noting that our box plots are not symmetrical about the median, meaning our data is skewed and may need a transformation. We'll do this by taking the natural log.

```{r}
# Visualizing OS data only with filter() to identify outlier
SPAD_Data_no_multiple |>
  filter(Treatment == "OS")

# Removing outlier data point with filter()
SPAD_Data_no_outlier = SPAD_Data_no_multiple |>
  filter(Num_leaves < 100.0)

# Visual verification by creating box plot with ggplot() + geom_boxplot()
SPAD_Data_no_outlier |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = Num_leaves) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Treatment), color = "black") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(x = "Treatment",
       y = "Number of leaves",
       title = "Number of leaves across all living plants per treatment"
  )

# Repeating plot with log transformation in aes() argument
SPAD_Data_no_outlier |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = log(Num_leaves)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Treatment), color = "black") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(x = "Treatment",
       y = "Log number of leaves",
       title = "Log number of leaves across all living plants per treatment"
  )
```

This looks better but our OS data are still very skewed despite the other three treatments now appearing symmetrical about the mean. We need to try another transformation, this time removing duplicate values of Num_leaves to thin out our data since this is the most likely candidate.

```{r}
# Thinning data with distinct() to remove duplicate data points that may be resulting in skew
SPAD_Data_no_outlier = SPAD_Data_no_outlier |>
  group_by(ID_num) |>
  distinct(Num_leaves, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Visualizing log-transformed box plot again with ggplot() + geom_boxplot()
SPAD_Data_no_outlier |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = log(Num_leaves)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Treatment), color = "black") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(x = "Treatment",
       y = "Log number of leaves"
  )
```

Thinning our data like this appears to have normalized things, so I'll conduct the ANOVA prerequisite tests now. A Bartlett test could not be used since all test have to account for both Treatment and Block, meaning we have to evaluate homogeneity of variance graphically, and we should consider our Shapiro-Wilk test results since our thinned data's sample size is small (n = 67).

```{r}
# Creating linear model for SPAD_Data_no_outlier with lm()
Leaf_model = lm(log(Num_leaves) ~ Treatment * Block, data = SPAD_Data_no_outlier)

# Checking QQ plot with plot() to evaluate normality
plot(Leaf_model, which = 2)

# Checking plot of residuals vs. fitted with plot() to check for homogeneity of variance
plot(Leaf_model, which = 1)

# Conducting Shapiro-Wilk test using shapiro.test() on model residuals
shapiro.test(Leaf_model$residuals)
```

Now, with our data cleaned, our QQ plot shows normality, our plot of residuals vs. fitted shows homoogeneity of variance, and our Shapiro-WIlk test further confirms normality (p \> 0.05). We can thus continue with a standard two-way ANOVA test.

### 2.3.3 Conducting Two-Way ANOVA test

```{r}
# Conducting two-way ANOVA on Leaf_model using aov()
Leaf_model_aov = aov(Num_leaves ~ Treatment * Block, data = SPAD_Data_no_outlier)

# Visual verification
Leaf_model_aov
```

Our degrees of freedom for our predictors and our residuals both make sense (# treatments - 1 = 3, 4 total treatments; \# blocks - 1 = 7, 8 total blocks; Residuals = 67 - (4 \* 7) = 39). We can thus comfortably apply a Tukey post-hoc test to the results.

# CHECK RESIDUAL D.O.F. WITH AMY

```{r}
# Conducting Tukey post-hoc test on results with TukeyHSD()
TukeyHSD(Leaf_model_aov)
```

results

### 2.3.4 Visualizing Results

```{r}
# Generating leaf count summary statistics with summarise()
Leaf_summary = SPAD_Data_no_outlier |>
  group_by(Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    mean_leaf = mean(Num_leaves),
    sd_leaf = sd(Num_leaves),
    n = n(),
    se_leaf = sd_leaf/sqrt(n)
  )

# Visual verification
Leaf_summary

# Visualizing ANOVA results with a column plot using ggplot() + geom_col()
Leaf_summary |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = mean_leaf, fill = Treatment) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_leaf - se_leaf,
    ymax = mean_leaf + se_leaf
    ),
    position = position_dodge(0.9), width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    label = c("ABD", "ABD", "C", "ABD"),
    vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1.75, position = "nudge"
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Leaf count"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

A column plot showing the mean leaf count of each treatment, with two-way ANOVA results denoted in text at the top of each column. Standard error is depicted via error bars also located at the top of each column. Results show no significant differences in mean leaf count between any of the treatments; only the natural recruits were found to have significantly heigher mean leaf count. It is possible that our natural recruits may have naturally gravitated toward ideal microclimate and thus been more successful in establishing within their plots, but we cannot infer this from leaf count alone.

## 2.4. ANOVA Testing on Height

### 2.4.1. Thinning data by selecting only the largest sapling at each tag

```{r}
# Filtering out data with multiple saplings with filter()
Height_Data_multiple = Height_Data_Clean |>
  group_by(Tag_Num) |>
  filter(is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == FALSE) |>
  
  # Selecting only the largest sapling from each tag with slice_max()
  slice_max(Seedling_Ht_cm) |>
  
  # Removing duplicate stragglers with distinct()
  distinct(Tag_Num, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Visual verification
Height_Data_multiple

# Generating intermediate tibble without multiple saplings using filter()
Height_Data_temp = Height_Data_Clean |>
  filter(is.na(Sapling_AB_etc) == TRUE)

# Visual verification
Height_Data_temp

# Reconstructing main data table by reattaching Height_Data_multiple to Height_Data_temp with bind_rows()
Height_Data_no_multiple = bind_rows(Height_Data_temp, Height_Data_multiple)

# Visual verification
Height_Data_no_multiple
```

### 2.4.2. Checking prerequisites for an ANOVA

```{r}
# Generating box plot of heights by treatment with ggplot() + geom_boxplot()
Height_Data_no_multiple |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = Seedling_Ht_cm) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Dead_Alive)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Seedling height (in cm)",
    fill = "Status"
  )
```

These box plots already show skew, varying unevenly about their median. We will check our data to see if there's more data that needs to be removed as in the leaf count ANOVA.

```{r}
# Visualizing data for NR and DT only with filter()
Height_Data_no_multiple |>
  filter(Treatment == "DT")

Height_Data_no_multiple |>
  filter(Treatment == "NR")
```

There does appear to be some duplicate values that we'll remove, but it's not certain that this will improve our data's normality.

```{r}
# Redoing box plot with log transformation applied to aes()
Height_Data_no_multiple |> ggplot() +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = log(Seedling_Ht_cm)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Dead_Alive)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Seedling height (in cm)",
    fill = "Status"
  )
```
